metadata.description: Learn ten prostate changes worth discussing with a healthcare professional, why symptoms do not confirm cancer and when to seek medical advice.
metadata.title: 10 Prostate Cancer Warning Signs You Shouldn't Ignore

landing.title: 10 Prostate Cancer Warning Signs You Shouldn't Ignore
landing.intro: Some prostate changes are easy to dismiss as ageing. Here are 10 warning signs worth knowing - including several that many men overlook.

disclaimer: General information only. This article is not a diagnosis, medical assessment or substitute for advice from a qualified healthcare professional.

sections.title: 10 Prostate Cancer Warning Signs
sections.intro: Prostate cancer often causes no symptoms at first. When changes do appear, they can overlap with common non-cancerous conditions, so symptoms alone cannot identify the cause.

points.title: Difficulty starting urination
paragraphs: You may take longer than usual to begin urinating, need to strain, or find that the flow is slow to start.
Benign prostate enlargement and other urinary conditions commonly cause this too. A change that is new, persistent or worsening still deserves assessment.

points.title: A weak or interrupted urine stream
paragraphs: The stream may feel weaker than it used to, stop and start, or take noticeably longer to finish.
Age-related prostate enlargement is a frequent explanation, but a continuing change should be discussed rather than assumed to be harmless.

points.title: Urinating more often, especially at night
paragraphs: You may need to urinate more frequently during the day or repeatedly wake at night to go.
Drinks, medicines, diabetes, bladder conditions and benign enlargement can all contribute. Seek advice when the pattern is new, persistent or disrupting daily life.

points.title: A sudden or difficult-to-control urge
paragraphs: An urge to urinate may arrive suddenly, feel unusually strong, or become harder to postpone than before.
Infection, medicines and bladder conditions can also cause urgency. A clinician can assess the full pattern when it keeps happening or becomes worse.

points.title: Feeling that the bladder has not emptied
paragraphs: You may finish urinating but still feel that you need to go, or find yourself returning to the toilet soon afterwards.
An enlarged prostate and several bladder problems can produce the same sensation. Repeated or worsening incomplete emptying should be checked.

points.title: New erectile difficulties
paragraphs: You may develop new difficulty getting or keeping an erection, particularly when this is different from your usual experience.
Erectile difficulties have many common physical and psychological causes. Mention a new or persistent change so it can be considered alongside any other symptoms.

points.title: Blood in the urine
paragraphs: Urine may look pink, red or brown, or a test may detect blood that was not visible.
Infection, stones and other urinary conditions are possible causes. Visible blood should be medically assessed even when it happens once or is painless.

points.title: Blood in semen or pain with ejaculation
paragraphs: Semen may appear blood-stained, or ejaculation may become painful when it was not before.
Infection, inflammation and other prostate conditions can cause these changes. They are not proof of cancer, but new or repeated episodes should be discussed with a clinician.

points.title: Persistent pain in the back, hips or pelvis
paragraphs: Prostate cancer that has spread can cause pain in the lower back, hips or pelvis that does not go away.
Muscle, joint and spinal problems are much more common explanations. Persistent, unexplained or worsening pain still needs medical assessment, especially alongside other changes.

points.title: Unexplained weight loss, tiredness or neurological changes
paragraphs: Advanced disease can sometimes be associated with losing weight without trying, marked tiredness, leg weakness or numbness, or changes in bladder or bowel control.
These symptoms have many other possible causes, but they should not be dismissed. New leg weakness or numbness, or loss of bladder or bowel control, needs urgent medical advice.

next.title: But Who Is Most At Risk?
next.copy: Symptoms are only part of the picture. Some men have a higher underlying risk because of factors they may not realise matter.

sections.title: Prostate Cancer Risk: 10 Things Worth Knowing
sections.intro: Risk is shaped by several factors, but no single factor can predict whether someone will develop prostate cancer.

points.title: Age
paragraphs: Age is the clearest established risk factor. Prostate cancer becomes more common as people get older and mostly affects men over 50.

points.title: Black ancestry
paragraphs: Men from Black African and African Caribbean backgrounds have a higher chance of developing prostate cancer. The reasons are complex and may include genetic, environmental and healthcare factors.

points.title: A father or brother diagnosed with prostate cancer
paragraphs: Risk can be higher when a father or brother has been diagnosed, although many people who develop prostate cancer have no known family history.

points.title: Several affected relatives
paragraphs: A pattern involving several relatives can be more significant than one isolated diagnosis, particularly when cases occur on the same side of the family.

points.title: Relatives diagnosed unusually young
paragraphs: Family history can carry more weight when prostate cancer was found at a relatively young age. A clinician may ask exactly who was affected and how old they were at diagnosis.

points.title: BRCA2
paragraphs: A harmful inherited change in the BRCA2 gene can increase prostate cancer risk. Genetic advice may be appropriate when a known BRCA2 change or a strong cancer pattern exists in the family.

points.title: Other inherited syndromes or genetic changes
paragraphs: Some other inherited changes, including those involved in DNA repair, can also raise risk. They account for only a minority of prostate cancers and usually need specialist interpretation.

points.title: A Wider Pattern Of Certain Cancers In The Family
paragraphs: Some inherited genetic changes can cause patterns of prostate, breast, ovarian, pancreatic or colorectal cancer across a family.

Having any one relative with one of these cancers does not automatically increase prostate-cancer risk. The combination of cancer types, ages at diagnosis and known genetic results is what may prompt further discussion.

points.title: Prostate symptoms or benign enlargement do not themselves mean cancer
paragraphs: Benign prostate enlargement and inflammation can cause urinary changes similar to those associated with prostate cancer. Having these symptoms does not by itself mean cancer is present, but a new or changing pattern still needs assessment.

points.title: Risk factors do not mean cancer will develop
paragraphs: Having one or several risk factors is not a diagnosis, and prostate cancer can also occur without obvious risk factors. A healthcare professional can help put personal risk into context.

sections.title: What Actually Happens During A Prostate Cancer Check?
sections.intro: There is no single test that answers every question. The pathway usually combines symptoms, history and test results, and the exact sequence can vary from person to person.

points.title: Symptoms and medical or family history
paragraphs: A clinician usually asks what has changed, when it began and whether it is getting worse. Medicines, previous urinary problems and relevant cancers in close relatives help put the symptoms and risk into context.

points.title: Urine testing and examination when appropriate
paragraphs: A urine test may look for infection, blood or another explanation for urinary symptoms. Depending on the situation, the clinician may also examine the abdomen or discuss a rectal examination of the prostate.

points.title: PSA blood test
paragraphs: A prostate-specific antigen test measures PSA in the blood. It can identify a possible prostate problem, but it cannot diagnose cancer on its own.

points.title: Interpreting or repeating PSA
paragraphs: PSA is interpreted alongside age, symptoms, examination findings and other risk information. It may be repeated when temporary factors or the overall result make that appropriate.

callouts.question: Does a high PSA mean cancer?
callouts.answer: No. A raised PSA can have several other causes.

callouts.question: Can PSA be raised for other reasons?
callouts.answer: Yes. Benign enlargement, inflammation and other factors can affect it.

callouts.question: Does everyone with a raised PSA need a biopsy?
callouts.answer: Not necessarily. PSA, MRI findings and other factors are considered together.

points.title: Multiparametric MRI
paragraphs: If specialist assessment is needed, a multiparametric MRI can provide detailed images of the prostate and show whether an area looks suspicious. The scan helps the team decide whether further investigation is needed.

points.title: Biopsy where needed
paragraphs: When more information is required after MRI and the wider assessment, a biopsy can take small tissue samples for examination under a microscope. It is used to confirm whether cancer is present and, if so, help determine its grade.

next.title: What Happens If Your Results Aren't Normal?
next.copy: See how raised PSA, suspicious MRI findings and biopsy results can shape what happens next.

sections.title: What Happens If Doctors Find Something?
sections.intro: An abnormal result is not automatically a cancer diagnosis. Doctors combine the available evidence before explaining what has been found and what choices come next.

points.title: Your PSA Is Raised — But Nothing Else Is Obvious
paragraphs: A raised PSA can have several causes and may be repeated or reviewed alongside symptoms, examination findings and personal risk. The next step depends on the whole picture rather than one number.

points.title: An MRI Finds Something Suspicious
paragraphs: MRI can identify an area that needs closer investigation, but a suspicious image does not by itself confirm cancer. The scan result helps specialists judge whether tissue sampling or another plan is appropriate.

points.title: Why A Biopsy Might Be Recommended
paragraphs: When MRI and the wider assessment suggest that cancer needs to be confirmed or excluded, a biopsy takes small prostate samples for examination. MRI usually comes before biopsy in the current NHS diagnostic pathway.

points.title: What Happens If Cancer Is Confirmed
paragraphs: A specialist team reviews the biopsy, scans, PSA and other information. They then explain the type of cancer, whether more staging tests are needed and which management options fit the individual situation.

points.title: What Grade Group And Stage Actually Mean
paragraphs: Grade Group describes how abnormal the cancer cells look and gives an indication of how they may behave. Stage describes how far the cancer has grown or spread; both help guide treatment and outlook discussions.

points.title: Does Prostate Cancer Always Need Treatment Straight Away?
paragraphs: No. Active surveillance uses planned tests and monitoring to delay or avoid treatment while retaining the possibility of curative treatment if the cancer changes.
Watchful waiting is a distinct, generally less intensive approach that focuses on controlling symptoms if they develop, rather than regular testing with the aim of later curative treatment.

points.title: The Main Treatment Routes Doctors May Discuss
paragraphs: Depending on stage, grade, general health and personal preferences, options may include monitoring, surgery, radiotherapy, hormone therapy, chemotherapy or other medicines. The benefits and possible side effects are considered with the specialist team.

next.title: How Treatable Is Prostate Cancer?
next.copy: The answer can be very different depending on whether the cancer is confined to the prostate or has spread, as well as its grade and other factors.

sections.title: Prostate Cancer Outlook: What Really Matters
sections.intro: Outlook can vary widely. Doctors consider several pieces of information together rather than relying on one symptom, scan or statistic.

points.title: Whether the cancer is localised
paragraphs: Cancer confined to the prostate generally has more potentially curative treatment options than disease that has spread. Its precise position and extent still matter when choosing an approach.

points.title: Whether it has grown outside the prostate
paragraphs: Cancer that has extended into nearby tissues is assessed differently from cancer contained entirely within the gland. Doctors consider exactly where it has grown and which treatments remain suitable.

points.title: Whether it has spread elsewhere
paragraphs: Spread to lymph nodes, bones or other organs changes the stage, treatment aims and outlook. Advanced prostate cancer can often still be controlled for a period of time, even when cure is not possible.

points.title: Grade Group and biological behaviour
paragraphs: Grade Group reflects how abnormal the cells look under a microscope and how aggressively the cancer may behave. A higher Grade Group generally suggests a greater likelihood of growth or spread.

points.title: PSA and other clinical information
paragraphs: PSA level and pattern can add useful context, but PSA is not interpreted alone. Doctors combine it with Grade Group, stage, scan findings and the amount of cancer identified.

points.title: Response to treatment
paragraphs: Follow-up PSA tests, scans, symptoms and other results show how the disease is responding. This information can change the next treatment decision over time.

points.title: Age and general health
paragraphs: Overall health, other medical conditions and ability to tolerate treatment all affect which options are appropriate. Personal preferences and likely side effects matter too.

points.title: Why earlier diagnosis may change the available options
paragraphs: Finding cancer before it has spread can make treatments intended to cure the disease possible for more people. Early diagnosis does not guarantee a particular outcome, but it can change the choices available.

points.title: Why statistics describe populations rather than individuals
paragraphs: Survival figures combine the experiences of large groups diagnosed in the past. They cannot predict exactly what will happen to one person or fully reflect individual biology, health and newer treatments.

conclusion.copy: Prostate cancer can behave very differently from one person to another. Symptoms, PSA or even one test result cannot tell you an individual's outlook on their own. Doctors combine several pieces of information before discussing what happens next.
